mainTopic: The argument between רב and שמואל about selling an ox that turns out to be a goring ox: do we follow the majority (רוב) in money cases, or does the claimant have to bring proof (המוציא מחבירו עליו הראיה)? Then a ברייתא shows that סומכוס and חכמים argue about an unclear goring case.
overview: The amud opens by finishing the search for a real difference between רב and שמואל about selling an ox that turns out to gore. The גמרא settles on a seller who can return the money. רב follows the majority, since most people buy oxen for plowing. שמואל says that in money matters we do not follow the majority, because המוציא מחבירו עליו הראיה. A ברייתא shows that סומכוס splits doubtful money, while חכמים require proof. רבי שמואל בר נחמני finds a פסוק for the burden of proof. רב אשי says logic already teaches that rule, so the פסוק is reassigned: it teaches that the court hears the claimant first. The Sages of נהרדעא add that sometimes the defendant is heard first. Then the גמרא turns to the משנה's cow that gored an ox, which seems to pay half plus a quarter. אביי explains these as a quarter and an eighth, in a case of two owners, and the גמרא works out who must prove a partnership. רבא rejects that reading and starts his own explanation with one owner, which continues on the next amud.

steps.title: If the seller can't repay, the buyer just keeps the ox
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the case: if the seller has no money, the buyer should simply keep the ox as payment, so the argument between רב and שמואל would change nothing.
steps.simpleTranslation: But if the seller has nothing to pay back with, the buyer should just keep the ox in place of his money. As people say: from someone who owes you, take even bran.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is still hunting for a case where רב and שמואל really disagree. It pushes back: in a case where the seller can't repay, there is no practical difference between them.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Say the sale is a מקח טעות (a mistaken sale), as רב holds. The buyer is owed his money back. But if the seller has no money, the buyer will end up keeping the ox as payment anyway. That is the same result as שמואל's view, where the sale stands, so the argument seems pointless.

phrases.english: But if there is nothing to be repaid from him,
let him take the ox in place of the money!
As people say:
From your debtors, collect even bran!
phrases.notes: A folk saying: when someone owes you, take whatever you can get, even something cheap.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִי לֵיכָּא לְאִשְׁתַּלּוֹמֵי מִינֵּיהּ, לִישְׁקְלֵיהּ לְתוֹרָא בְּזוּזֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the earlier search on the דף for a case where רב and שמואל disagree in practice.
steps.kashyaTarget: The case where the seller has no money to give back.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Even if רב is right that the sale is cancelled, the buyer keeps the ox in place of his money. So the result is the same as שמואל's, and there is no real disagreement.

steps.title: The argument is about a seller who can repay
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that רב and שמואל argue about a case where the seller does have money to return.
steps.simpleTranslation: No, the argument is needed for a case where the seller does have money to pay back.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge by narrowing the case. The seller has money, and the buyer wants his money back instead of the ox.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Now there is a real difference between the two views. According to רב, the buyer gets his money back. According to שמואל, the sale stands and the buyer is stuck with the ox.

keyTerms.meaning: it is only needed for (this case)

phrases.english: No, it is needed
where there is money to be repaid from him.

steps.terutzHavaAmina: The argument seemed to make no practical difference, because the buyer could always keep the ox.
steps.terutzMaskana: The argument is about a seller who can repay, so the outcome really does depend on whose view we follow.

steps.title: רב: follow the majority, so the sale was a mistake
steps.stepSummary: רב rules it is a מקח טעות, because we follow the majority, and most people buy oxen for plowing.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב says this is a mistaken sale. Go after the majority, and most people buy oxen for plowing.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now explains the reasoning behind רב's view.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Nobody said out loud why the buyer wanted the ox. רב fills in that gap with the majority (רוב): most buyers want a plowing ox. A goring ox is no good for plowing, so the buyer did not get what he paid for, and the sale is cancelled.

keyTerms.meaning: a mistaken sale, which can be cancelled

phrases.english: Rav says:
This is a mistaken sale,
go after the majority,
and the majority of people
buy oxen for plowing.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב אָמַר הֲרֵי זֶה מִקָּח טָעוּת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Now that the case is clear, the גמרא explains רב's reasoning.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: We use the majority to decide what the buyer intended, so the sale of a goring ox is a מקח טעות.

steps.title: שמואל: the seller can say he sold it for slaughter
steps.stepSummary: שמואל says the seller can claim he sold the ox for slaughter, and we do not follow the majority.
steps.simpleTranslation: שמואל says the seller can tell him, 'I sold it to you for slaughter,' and we do not follow the majority.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains שמואל's side. The seller can claim the ox was sold for meat, and then its goring does not matter.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the ox was sold for שחיטה, a goring habit is not a defect, so the sale stands. שמואל does not let the majority of buyers decide the question against the seller.

phrases.english: And Shmuel says:
He can say to him,
"I sold it to you for slaughter,"
and we do not follow the majority.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the opposite view to רב's in step 3.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The seller's claim that he sold the ox for slaughter is accepted, and the majority does not overrule it.

steps.title: Majority decides prohibitions, not money cases
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains why שמואל does not use the majority: רוב is used for איסור questions, but in money cases the claimant must bring proof.
steps.simpleTranslation: When do we follow the majority? In questions of what is forbidden or permitted. But in money matters we do not follow the majority. Instead, whoever wants to take money from his fellow must bring proof.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the principle behind שמואל's view: רוב works for איסור, but not for ממון.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In money cases, the money stays with whoever is holding it now. The buyer wants his money back from the seller, so the buyer is the המוציא מחבירו (the one trying to take money from someone else). A majority does not count as proof for him, so he loses.

keyTerms.meaning: matters of what is forbidden or permitted
whoever wants to take money from another must bring proof

steps.whatToRemember: רב: in this case we follow the majority, so the sale is cancelled. שמואל: רוב is used in איסור, but in ממון the claimant needs real proof.
steps.confusionAlert: שמואל is not saying the majority is never used. He uses it for איסור questions, just not to take money away from someone.
steps.whyThisMatters: The split between רוב in איסור and proof in ממון is a basic rule that comes up throughout ש״ס.

phrases.english: When do we follow the majority?
In matters of prohibition.
But in money matters,
we do not follow the majority.
Rather, one who takes money from his fellow,
the proof is upon him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the reason behind שמואל's statement in step 4.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רוב decides questions of איסור. In money cases the claimant must bring proof, and a majority is not enough.

steps.title: ברייתא: סומכוס splits the payment, חכמים require proof
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא supports the earlier claim that the משנה follows סומכוס. When it is unclear whether a cow gave birth before or after it was gored, סומכוס has the owner pay a quarter-damage for the calf, while חכמים require the claimant to bring proof.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is also taught this way: an ox gored a cow, and the cow's fetus was found next to it. Nobody knows if the cow gave birth before or after the goring. The ox's owner pays half-damage for the cow and quarter-damage for the calf. This is the view of סומכוס. חכמים say: whoever wants to take money from his fellow must bring proof.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא to support רב יהודה's earlier statement that the משנה follows סומכוס.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The calf is a doubt: maybe it was hurt by the goring, maybe it was born before. סומכוס splits the doubtful money, so instead of half-damage the owner pays half of that, a quarter. חכמים say that without proof, the cow's owner gets nothing for the calf.
steps.whatToRemember: סומכוס splits money when there is a doubt. חכמים say המוציא מחבירו עליו הראיה, the same principle שמואל used.

phrases.english: It is also taught so:
An ox that gored a cow,
and its fetus was found beside it,
and he does not know
whether it gave birth before it gored it
or gave birth after it gored it:
he pays half-damage for the cow
and quarter-damage for the offspring.
These are the words of Sumakhos.
And the Sages say:
One who takes from his fellow, the proof is upon him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Goes back to רב יהודה's statement, made earlier on the דף, that the משנה follows סומכוס.
steps.raayaObject: רב יהודה's claim that the משנה about the cow and its fetus follows סומכוס.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא where סומכוס rules half-damage for the cow and quarter-damage for the calf, and חכמים say המוציא מחבירו עליו הראיה.

steps.title: A verse as the source that the claimant must bring proof
steps.stepSummary: רבי שמואל בר נחמני learns המוציא מחבירו עליו הראיה from the פסוק 'מי בעל דברים יגש אלהם', reading it as 'he should bring proof to them.'
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי שמואל בר נחמני said: How do we know that the person who wants to take money from someone else must bring proof? Because the פסוק says, 'Whoever has a case, let him come near to them.' Read it as: let him bring proof to them.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a source in the תורה for the rule from Step 5: in money cases, the one making the claim must bring proof.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק says יִגַּשׁ, 'he will come near.' רבי שמואל בר נחמני reads it as יַגִּישׁ, 'he will bring near,' meaning he must bring proof to the judges. So the person with the claim carries the burden.

keyTerms.meaning: One who wants to take money or property from another person (the claimant)
The burden of proof is on him
A person who has a case or claim

phrases.english: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani said:
From where do we know that one who takes from his fellow
must bring the proof?
As it says: "Whoever has a case
let him come near to them"
meaning, let him bring proof near to them.
phrases.notes: He reads 'come near' (יִגַּשׁ) as 'bring near' (יַגִּישׁ), a small change in the vowels.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a תורה source for the rule mentioned in Step 5, that in money cases the claimant must bring proof.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The rule המוציא מחבירו עליו הראיה comes from 'מי בעל דברים יגש אלהם', read as 'let him bring proof to them.'

steps.title: Why do we need a verse when logic teaches it?
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי objects: we do not need a פסוק for this rule. It is plain logic, just as the person in pain is the one who goes to the doctor.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אשי challenged this: Why do I need a פסוק for this? It is simple logic. The person who is in pain is the one who goes to the doctor.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי attacks Step 7. He says the rule is so obvious from common sense that a פסוק is not needed to teach it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The person with the problem is the one who has to fix it. The person in pain goes to the doctor, and the person who wants money must prove his claim. If logic already teaches the rule, the פסוק must be teaching something else.

keyTerms.meaning: He challenges it (an objection is coming)
Why do I need a verse?

phrases.english: Rav Ashi objects to this:
Why do I need a verse for this?
It is logic:
the one who has the pain
is the one who goes to the doctor!

steps.triggerLanguage: מַתְקֵיף לַהּ רַב אָשֵׁי: הָא לְמָה לִי קְרָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges Step 7's use of the פסוק as the source for the burden of proof.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי שמואל בר נחמני's use of the פסוק for המוציא מחבירו עליו הראיה
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A פסוק is not needed for something logic already teaches. The person with the problem obviously has to deal with it.

steps.title: The verse teaches that the court hears the claimant first
steps.stepSummary: Since logic already teaches the burden of proof, the פסוק is used for רב נחמן's rule in the name of רבה בר אבוה: the court hears the claimant's words first.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, the פסוק teaches what רב נחמן said in the name of רבה בר אבוה: How do we know that the court listens to the claimant first? Because the פסוק says, 'Whoever has a case, let him come near to them.' This means he should bring his words to them first.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא accepts רב אשי's point and finds a new job for the פסוק. It teaches the order of a court case: the claimant speaks first.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Now יַגִּישׁ is read as 'let him bring his words,' not 'let him bring proof.' The burden of proof stays a matter of logic. The פסוק teaches a separate rule about who presents his side first.

keyTerms.meaning: The court attends to, deals with

steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix up the two rules. 'The claimant must bring proof' (from logic) is about who must prove. 'The claimant is heard first' (from the פסוק) is about the order in court.

phrases.english: Rather, the verse is needed for the teaching of Rav Nachman
that Rabbah bar Avuh said,

phrases.aramaic: דְּאָמַר רַב נַחְמָן אָמַר רַבָּה בַּר אֲבוּהּ:
phrases.english: as Rav Nachman said that Rabbah bar Avuh said:
From where do we know that the court does not attend
to anyone but the claimant first?
As it says: "Whoever has a case, let him come near to them"
meaning, let him bring his words to them first.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא קְרָא לְכִדְרַב נַחְמָן אָמַר רַבָּה בַּר אֲבוּהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רב אשי's challenge by giving the פסוק a different job.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reassigning the verse to a different teaching
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The פסוק was thought to teach the burden of proof.
steps.terutzMaskana: The burden of proof comes from logic. The פסוק teaches that the court hears the claimant first.
steps.whyThisMatters: It sets the standard order of a court case: the claimant presents his claim first.

steps.title: Sometimes the defendant is heard first
steps.stepSummary: The Sages of נהרדעא say there are times the court hears the נתבע first. This happens when his property is losing value because of the claim.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Sages of נהרדעא said: Sometimes the court listens to the defendant first. When is that? When his property is going down in value.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא adds an exception to the rule from Step 9 and then explains when the exception applies.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally the claimant goes first. But if the claim is making the defendant's property lose value, the court hears him first. That way the matter can be cleared up quickly and he does not keep losing money.

keyTerms.meaning: The Sages of the city נהרדעא
The defendant, the one being sued
What is the case? (asking for the exact situation)

steps.whatToRemember: The claimant must bring proof (logic). The claimant is heard first (the פסוק). But if the defendant's property is losing value, the defendant may be heard first (נהרדעא).

phrases.english: The Sages of Nehardea say:
Sometimes the court attends to the defendant first.
And what is the case?
Where his property is dropping in value.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמְרִי נְהַרְדָּעֵי: פְּעָמִים שֶׁנִּזְקָקִין לַנִּתְבָּע תְּחִלָּה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Limits the rule of Step 9 by giving an exception where the defendant goes first.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: When the defendant's property is losing value because of the claim, the court may hear the defendant first.

steps.title: Why does the cow's owner pay three-quarters?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה about a cow that gored an ox. It asks how the משנה can require 'half damage and quarter damage', which adds up to three-quarters, when a תם only ever pays half.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה says: 'And likewise, a cow that gored an ox, etc.' Half damage AND quarter damage?! He only has to pay half damage! What is three-quarters doing here?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes a new line of the משנה. It points out that the משנה's numbers seem to add up to more than the law allows.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An ox that is a תם pays only חצי נזק. Read simply, the משנה charges half from the cow plus a quarter from the calf, which makes three-quarters. That cannot be right, so the גמרא asks what the משנה really means.

keyTerms.meaning: Half of the damage. This is what a תם pays.
Literally 'what is its business?' It means: what is this doing here?

steps.confusionAlert: Don't assume the משנה means three-quarters of the full damage. The whole question is that this is too much, and אביי will explain that the real numbers are smaller.

phrases.english: And likewise, a cow that gored the ox, etc.
Half damage and quarter damage?!
It is only half damage that he needs to pay!
The full damage minus a quarter,
what is it doing here?

steps.triggerLanguage: חֲצִי נֶזֶק וּרְבִיעַ נֶזֶק?! פַּלְגָא נִזְקָא הוּא דְּבָעֵי שַׁלּוֹמֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new section of the משנה, moving on from the discussion of the burden of proof.
steps.kashyaTarget: The משנה's wording 'חצי נזק and רביע נזק' in the cow-and-calf case.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A תם pays at most half the damage. Half plus a quarter is three-quarters, which is more than the law allows.

steps.title: The real numbers are one-quarter and one-eighth
steps.stepSummary: אביי explains that the משנה's 'half' means half of the half-payment, which is one-quarter of the damage. Its 'quarter' means one-eighth of the damage.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said: 'Half damage' means one out of four parts of the damage. 'Quarter damage' means one out of eight parts of the damage.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי answers the question by explaining that the משנה is counting fractions of the normal half-payment, not fractions of the whole damage.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The normal payment for a תם is half the damage. Because the calf may have been inside the cow at the time, the two animals might share the blame, so the cow pays half of that half, which is one-quarter. The calf's share is the other quarter, but since it is unclear whether the calf was even there, it pays only half of that share, which is one-eighth. This fits the view of סומכוס from step 6, that money in doubt is split.

keyTerms.meaning: One out of four, meaning one-quarter.
One out of eight, meaning one-eighth.

steps.whatToRemember: The cow pays one-quarter of the damage and the calf pays one-eighth, so the total is three-eighths. That stays under the half-damage limit of a תם.

phrases.english: Abaye said:
'Half damage' means one out of four of the damage,
phrases.notes: He means half of the normal half-payment, paid from the cow.

phrases.english: and 'quarter damage' means one out of eight of the damage.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר אַבָּיֵי: חֲצִי נֶזֶק – אֶחָד מֵאַרְבָּעָה בַּנֶּזֶק
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 11 by explaining the משנה's fractions differently.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Explains the wording: the משנה's fractions are measured from the half-payment, not from the full damage.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The משנה means half of the full damage plus a quarter of the full damage, which is three-quarters.
steps.terutzMaskana: The cow pays one-quarter and the calf pays one-eighth, for a total of three-eighths.

steps.title: If one person owns both animals, why split the payment?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks: if the cow and calf belong to the same person, the injured man can just tell him to pay the full half, since either way his own animal did the damage.
steps.simpleTranslation: But if the cow and the calf belong to one person, then the injured man can say to the cow's owner: 'Whichever way you look at it, give me half damage.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges אביי's split. It says splitting the payment makes no sense if one person owns both animals.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Splitting between the cow and the calf only matters if someone can say 'not my animal.' If both animals belong to the same owner, then whether the cow did it alone or together with the calf, his animals caused the damage. So he should simply pay the full half damage.

keyTerms.meaning: Whichever way you look at it. Both possibilities lead to the same result.

phrases.english: But if the cow and the calf belong to one person,

phrases.aramaic: הָכִי נָמֵי דְּמָצֵי אָמַר לֵיהּ לְבַעַל פָּרָה:
phrases.english: then he can indeed say to the cow's owner:
phrases.notes: 'He' is the injured man, the owner of the ox that was gored.

phrases.aramaic: מִמָּה נַפְשָׁךְ, חֲצִי נֶזֶק הַב לִי.
phrases.english: 'Whichever way you look at it, give me half damage.'

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִי פָּרָה וּוָלָד דְּחַד נִינְהוּ – הָכִי נָמֵי דְּמָצֵי אָמַר לֵיהּ לְבַעַל פָּרָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the split payment that אביי described in step 12.
steps.kashyaTarget: אביי's split between the cow and the calf.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: With a single owner, either possibility makes him responsible for the full half damage, so there is nothing to split.

steps.title: The case is where the cow and calf have different owners
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the משנה is talking about a case where one person owns the cow and a different person owns the calf.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, the משנה is only needed for a case where the cow belongs to one person and the calf belongs to another.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge by narrowing the משנה's case to two different owners.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When there are two owners, each one can push part of the blame onto the other animal. That is why the payment really does get split between the cow and the calf. With a single owner, the משנה's ruling would not be needed.

keyTerms.meaning: It is not needed except for this case. The ruling is only needed for a specific situation.
Rather. It introduces the corrected understanding.

phrases.english: Rather, it is only needed
where the cow belongs to one person and the calf to another.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא לָא צְרִיכָא, דְּפָרָה דְּחַד, וּוָלָד דְּחַד
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 13 by limiting the משנה to a case with two owners.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Narrows the case: the משנה is limited to a situation with two separate owners.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: One person might own both the cow and the calf.
steps.terutzMaskana: The cow and the calf have different owners, so the split payment makes sense.

steps.title: The cow's owner should have to prove he has a partner
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges again: if the injured man claims from the cow's owner first, he can say that the cow certainly did damage, so the cow's owner must prove that the calf was a partner.
steps.simpleTranslation: But if the injured man claimed from the cow's owner first, he can say to him: 'Your cow damaged me. Bring me proof that you have partners.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא raises a new problem even in the two-owner case. The next step answers it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The cow surely gored. The only question is whether the calf, which was possibly still inside the cow, shares the blame. Based on the rule from step 5 that the one who wants to take money away from someone must bring proof, the cow's owner is the one trying to get out of paying the full half. So it seems he should have to prove that the calf was a partner, or else pay the whole half damage.

keyTerms.meaning: Partners. Here this means the calf as a partner in the goring.

steps.whyThisMatters: This connects the cow-and-calf case to the burden-of-proof discussion. It also explains why the order of who gets sued first could change the result.

phrases.aramaic: וְאִי דִּקְדֵים תַּבְעֵיהּ לְבַעַל פָּרָה תְּחִלָּה –
phrases.english: But if he went ahead and claimed from the cow's owner first,

phrases.aramaic: הָכִי נָמֵי דְּאָמַר לֵיהּ לְבַעַל פָּרָה:
phrases.english: then he can indeed say to the cow's owner:
'Your cow damaged me,'

phrases.aramaic: הַב לִי רְאָיָה דְּאִית לָךְ שׁוּתָּפֵי.
phrases.english: 'bring me proof that you have partners.'
phrases.notes: He means proof that the calf was still inside the cow during the goring, which would make it a partner in the damage.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִי דִּקְדֵים תַּבְעֵיהּ לְבַעַל פָּרָה תְּחִלָּה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the two-owner case from step 14.
steps.kashyaTarget: The split payment in the two-owner case.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The cow certainly did damage, so its owner is the one trying to reduce what he owes. Under the rule that the one taking money from another must bring proof, he must prove the calf was a partner, or else pay the full half.

steps.title: The injured man claimed from the calf's owner first
steps.stepSummary: The משנה's case is one where the injured man first claimed from the calf's owner. That shows he admits there is a partner, so the cow's owner pays only his share.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, the case is where he first claimed from the calf's owner. Then the cow's owner can say to him: 'You showed what you think, that I have a partner.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge from step 15 by changing the case: the injured man went to the calf's owner first.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In step 15 the problem was that the injured man could claim the whole half-payment from the cow's owner. Now the case is narrowed. Because he went after the calf's owner first, he admitted the calf may have shared in the damage. So the cow's owner can refuse to pay more than his own share.

keyTerms.meaning: He claimed from him (made a demand for payment)
You revealed your opinion, you showed what you think
A partner, someone who shares in the damage

phrases.english: Rather, it is where he first claimed
phrases.notes: 'He' is the injured man, the owner of the ox that was hurt.

phrases.english: from the owner of the calf first,
so that he can say to him:
phrases.notes: The speaker now is the cow's owner, answering the injured man.

phrases.english: You revealed your opinion
that I have a partner.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא דִּקְדֵים תַּבְעֵיהּ לְבַעַל וָלָד תְּחִלָּה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 15 by narrowing the case.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Narrowing the case (the order of the claims)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The cow's owner could be forced to pay the whole half-payment, since his cow certainly did damage.
steps.terutzMaskana: Because the injured man claimed from the calf's owner first, he admitted there is a partner. The cow's owner pays only his share.

steps.title: Another version: the cow's owner can push off the claim either way
steps.stepSummary: Another version says that even if the injured man claimed from the cow's owner first, the cow's owner can push him off by saying he knows he has a partner.
steps.simpleTranslation: Some say: even if he first claimed from the cow's owner, that owner can push him off, because he can say: 'I know that I have a partner.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a second version of the answer. In this version the order of the claims does not matter.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the first version, the cow's owner could split the payment only if the injured man had gone to the calf's owner first. Here, the cow's owner's own knowledge that the calf shared in the damage is enough to push off the full claim. So the משנה's reduced payment works even without the special order of claims.

keyTerms.meaning: He can push him off, he can turn away his claim

phrases.english: There are those who say:
even though he first claimed
from the owner of the cow first,
he can push him off,
for he can say to him:
I certainly know
that I have a partner.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִיכָּא דְּאָמְרִי: אַף עַל גַּב דִּקְדֵים תַּבְעֵיהּ לְבַעַל פָּרָה תְּחִלָּה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second version that replaces step 16's answer. It rejects the challenge of step 15 outright instead of narrowing the case.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Rejecting the premise of the challenge
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The injured man can collect everything from the cow's owner if he claims from him first.
steps.terutzMaskana: The cow's owner can always push him off, since he knows he has a partner.

steps.title: רבא objects that the משנה says half and quarter, not quarter and eighth
steps.stepSummary: רבא challenges אביי: the משנה does not say 'one-quarter' and 'one-eighth.' It says 'half' and 'quarter.'
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: Does the משנה teach 'one-quarter of the damage' and 'one-eighth of the damage'? It teaches 'half damage' and 'quarter damage'!
steps.whatsHappening: רבא attacks אביי's whole explanation from step 12 by looking at the plain words of the משנה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: אביי read the משנה's 'half' as a quarter and its 'quarter' as an eighth. רבא says this twists the words. If the משנה meant a quarter and an eighth, it would have said so.

keyTerms.meaning: Is that to say? (a question that expects 'no')
It teaches, it says (about the wording of the משנה)

phrases.english: Rava said:
Is that to say it teaches 'one-quarter of the damage'
and 'one-eighth of the damage'?
phrases.notes: These are the amounts אביי said the משנה really meant, back in step 12.

phrases.english: It teaches 'half damage' and 'quarter damage'!

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רָבָא: אַטּוּ ״אֶחָד מֵאַרְבָּעָה בַּנֶּזֶק״ וְ״אֶחָד מִשְּׁמֹנָה בַּנֶּזֶק״ קָתָנֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the discussion of אביי's case and attacks אביי's basic reading of the משנה.
steps.kashyaTarget: אביי's explanation (step 12) that 'half' means a quarter and 'quarter' means an eighth.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The משנה's plain words say half and quarter. Reading them as a quarter and an eighth does not fit the text.

steps.title: רבא's new reading: one owner, and the payment comes from the animal itself
steps.stepSummary: רבא explains that the cow and calf belong to one person. If the cow is available, the half-payment is collected from the cow.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, רבא said: The case really is where the cow and calf belong to one person. This is what we mean: if the cow is there, the half-payment is collected from the cow.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא offers his own explanation of the משנה, keeping 'half' as a real half. His explanation continues on the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Unlike אביי, רבא says one person owns both animals, so the words 'half' and 'quarter' keep their simple meaning. His point rests on the rule that a תם pays only from the value of the animal that did the damage. So the משנה is telling us which animal the payment can be collected from.

keyTerms.meaning: Really, actually (going back to a reading that was set aside)
And this is what we are saying
It is paid, it is collected

steps.confusionAlert: רבא is not saying the cow's owner pays a total of three-quarters. He is explaining which animal the payment is collected from, and the explanation continues on the next amud.
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets up רבא's main idea: the משנה's numbers are about where the money is collected from, not about adding extra payments.

phrases.english: Rather, Rava said:
Really, it is about a cow and calf belonging to one person,
and this is what we are saying:
if the cow is there,
half damage is collected from the cow.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא אָמַר רָבָא: לְעוֹלָם בְּפָרָה וּוָלָד דְּחַד
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רבא's own challenge from step 18 with a new reading that keeps the משנה's wording as it is.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Re-reading the משנה (one owner, with the numbers telling where the payment is collected from)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: With one owner, the numbers would add up to three-quarters, which is more than a תם pays (step 11). With two owners (אביי), the words have to be stretched.
steps.terutzMaskana: One owner. The half-payment is collected from the cow if it is available. The rest of the explanation continues on the next amud.
